react_lesson_1.title: Introduction to React
react_lesson_1.description: Learn what React is, JSX basics, and components

react_lesson_1:slide:0.title: What is React? ⚛️
react_lesson_1:slide:0.content:
React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Created by Facebook, it lets you build complex UIs from small, reusable pieces called components.

Why React?
• Component-based architecture
• Virtual DOM for fast updates
• Large ecosystem and community
• Used by Facebook, Netflix, Instagram

react_lesson_3.title: State Management
react_lesson_3.description: Learn useState hook, state updates, and controlled components

react_lesson_3:slide:0.title: Understanding State 🔄
react_lesson_3:slide:0.content:
State is data that changes over time. Unlike props, state is managed within the component.

When state changes:
• React re-renders the component
• UI updates automatically
• User interactions can modify state

Use the useState hook to add state!

react_lesson_3:slide:1.title: The useState Hook
react_lesson_3:slide:1.content: useState returns current state and an updater function:

react_lesson_3:question:2.explanation: Always use the setState function returned by useState. Never modify state directly.

react_lesson_4.title: Handling Events
react_lesson_4.description: Master onClick, onChange, and form handling

react_lesson_4:slide:0.title: React Events 🖱️
react_lesson_4:slide:0.content:
React handles events similar to HTML, but with camelCase naming:

• onClick (not onclick)
• onChange (not onchange)
• onSubmit (not onsubmit)

Event handlers are functions, not strings!
<button onClick={handleClick}> ✅
<button onClick="handleClick()"> ❌

react_lesson_4:question:1.explanation: e.preventDefault() stops the default form submission behavior which would reload the page.

react_lesson_4:question:2.prompt: How do you pass parameters to an event handler?
react_lesson_4:question:2.explanation: Wrap the function call in an arrow function to pass parameters: onClick={() => handleClick(param)}

react_lesson_4:question:3.explanation: The event object provides details about the event, including the target element, event type, and helpful methods.

react_lesson_5.title: Lists & Keys
react_lesson_5.description: Render lists with .map() and understand unique keys

react_lesson_5:slide:0.title: Rendering Lists 📋
react_lesson_5:slide:0.content:
Use JavaScript's .map() to render lists of elements:

• Transform array data into JSX
• Each item needs a unique "key" prop
• Keys help React identify which items changed
• Keys should be stable and unique

react_lesson_5:slide:2.title: Understanding Keys
react_lesson_5:slide:2.content: Keys help React identify list items efficiently:

react_lesson_5:question:0.prompt: Which method is used to render lists in React?
react_lesson_5:question:0.explanation: .map() transforms an array into a new array of JSX elements, making it perfect for rendering lists.

react_lesson_5:question:1.prompt: Why do list items need a key prop?
react_lesson_5:question:1.explanation: Keys help React identify which items have changed, been added, or removed, enabling efficient updates.

options.react_lesson_5:question:1:option:1: To help React identify which items changed

react_lesson_5:question:2.explanation: Good keys are stable and unique identifiers like database IDs, not array indices which can change.

options.react_lesson_5:question:2:option:2: A stable, unique identifier like an ID

react_lesson_5:question:3.prompt: When can you use index as a key?
react_lesson_5:question:3.explanation: Index can be used as a last resort for static lists that won't reorder, but unique IDs are always better.

options.react_lesson_5:question:3:option:2: Only if the list is static and won't reorder

react_lesson_5:question:4.prompt: Do keys need to be globally unique?
react_lesson_5:question:4.explanation: Keys only need to be unique among siblings (items in the same list), not globally across the app.

options.react_lesson_5:question:4:option:3: They don't need to be unique

react_lesson_7.description: Master side effects, cleanup, and dependencies

react_lesson_7:slide:0.title: Understanding Side Effects 🌊
react_lesson_7:slide:0.content:
Side effects are operations that reach outside your component:

• Fetching data from APIs
• Setting up subscriptions
• Manually changing the DOM
• Setting timers

useEffect runs after render, keeping your component pure!

react_lesson_8.title: Building a Todo App

react_lesson_8:slide:0.title: Project Planning 🎯
react_lesson_8:slide:0.content:
Let's build a todo app combining everything you've learned:

• State management (useState)
• Form handling (events)
• Lists and keys (.map)
• Conditional rendering
• Component composition

This is where it all comes together!

react_lesson_8:question:1.prompt: How do you add a new item to an array in state?
react_lesson_8:question:1.explanation: Use the spread operator to create a new array: setTodos([...todos, newItem]). Never mutate state directly.

react_lesson_8:question:2.explanation: Date.now() returns the current timestamp in milliseconds, making it useful for generating simple unique IDs.

react_lesson_8:question:3.prompt: How do you update a specific item in an array?
react_lesson_8:question:3.explanation: Use .map() to iterate and conditionally update the specific item, creating a new array without mutating state.
